title: How Old Can You Get?
text: So, how old can you get? When people die of old age, they really die from age-related diseases like heart issues, cancer, or respiratory diseases. Sadly, most of them can't be cured today, but let's assume for a minute that they could be in the near future. As soon as an organ fails, we could replace it and live on for as long as we want it, right? Here's the bad news. There's a passionate scientific debate around whether or not there's a limit to the human lifespan. Scientists currently place this limit around 120 years and think it's linked to human biochemistry. When we age, the DNA in ourselves loses its ability to multiply, which limits the amount of damage our bodies can repair. So, what's the good news? Science has made huge progress in aging research and found many promising tools that might slow, stop, or reverse aging. And, without aging, death might be postponed much longer, pushing our limit to 200 years without any trouble. To live even longer, we'd have to change our entire biochemistry. But then, would we still be human? Human.

title: How To Build A Matchbox Camera
text: Slide out the tray and cut a small window in its center. Then cut a smaller hole in the outer sleeve, color the inside's black, and tape a square of soda can over the hole. Poke a tiny pinhole through the aluminum and cover it with tape to make a shutter. In complete darkness, run 35 millimeter film through the box and tape its end to an empty film canister. Slide the tray back in, seal every gap with electrical tape, and add a ring to help line the film. Point it at your subjects, uncover the pinhole for a few seconds, cover it again, then wind the film forward, and once developed, you'll have a photograph.

title: ONE Gene Determines How Many Fingers You Have
text: Will your grandchildren have six fingers? Polydactyly is the condition of having extra fingers and toes, and it's among the most common genetic conditions occurring in about 1 in 1000 babies. It's harmless and comes in many different forms, from extra pinky fingers to extra thumbs, from stubs to fully developed fingers and toes. And while some people get stubs removed, others with extra fingers use them to rock out with sick guitar solos. Polydactyly of all kinds is seen around the world. While children with European and Asian ancestry are more likely to be born with double thumbs, what would you do if you have an extra finger? Give four thumbs up, wear 12 ring pops, and while many human traits like hair colour are controlled by a big complicated mix of genes, Polydactyly is controlled by just one. That gene is also dominant, making it very easy to inherit and the condition often runs in families. So even if you have five fingers, who knows?

title: Rifle with a built in bottle opener?
text: Some guns are accurate at long range. Some guns are compact and easy to carry. Some guns make it easy to have a drink. From bottle openers and wire cutters to cleaning kits and magazine loaders, here's a few examples of firearms that have hidden features that make the soldier's life a little bit easier. The Gileo Bottle Open Arm If there was a multi-purpose firearm, it would have to be the Gileo. After the Six-Day War in 1967, the Israeli Defense Force or IDF needed a replacement for the FAL, whose performance was underwhelming. After studying captured AKs, the end result was the Gileo. As an aside, the Gileo was based on the AK-47, invented by Mikhail Kailashnikov. By a bit of historical irony, Gileo's inventor was Yizarel Balashnikov. Anyway, the Gileo was chambered in 5.56mm and it came in three variants, the standard automatic rifle machine gun, an automatic rifle, and a short automatic rifle, though other variants would follow in the later years. It was designed to be as ergonomic as possible, with the charging handle protruding from the upper receiver, so left or right-handed shooters can use it with equal efficiency, and also had a folding carry handle. One of the more noteworthy features, however, has nothing to do with the function of the firearm. IDF troops had a bad habit of using the front lip of magazines as bottle openers, which would damage the thin metal. To prevent equipment damage, the Gileo came equipped with a built-in bottle opener. Located at the base of the foregrip, it's, well, a bottle opener. This isn't a part that can be improvised as a bottle opener, but a dedicated purpose-built new feature that was added in purely for a soldier's benefit, and to protect the equipment from damage due to improper use. That's not the only hidden feature of the Gileo. On the ARM variant, the attached bipod can be rotated against an extension and used as a wire cutter to clear barbed wire. Though the Gileo was the Swiss Army knife of firearms, it was eventually replaced by the M16 series of weapons, being eventually relegated to support roles until taken out of service. One thing all of these hidden features have in common is that they don't make the weapon dramatically more powerful. They simply solve everyday problems in clever ways. A bottle opener saves your magazines. A wire cutter means carrying one less tool. Small ideas that make life just a little easier.
